metaTitle: Best Worm Drive Circular Saws in 2026
metaDescription: Six worm drive and rear handle circular saws compared on gearing, weight, blade size, bevel range and oil bath design, for framing and heavy ripping.
expertTake: The SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 is the worm drive saw most framers should buy, with a magnesium body, a 15 amp motor and a depth setting system built for speed. The Bosch CSW41 is the value pick among the true worm drives. If you mostly make short crosscuts in softwood, skip worm drives, because a lighter sidewinder is faster and easier to carry.
introParagraphs: A worm drive saw puts the motor behind the blade and drives it through a pair of gears set at ninety degrees. The result is more torque, a longer body and a blade on the left, which suits long rips and wet or dense lumber.
This guide explains how worm and hypoid gearing work, why weight and oil changes matter and where cordless rear handle saws now compete.

products.name: SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 15 Amp 7-1/4 Inch Magnesium Worm Drive Saw
products.description:
The SPT77WML-01 is the lightest magnesium bodied worm drive in the SKILSAW line, with a 15 amp motor and a 53 degree bevel. Its cut-ready depth system lets you read the depth of cut from the front, which speeds up setup. The blade sits on the left for right handed users, which gives a clear view of the line.

Compared with the aluminum SPT77W-01, which weighs 14.2 lb without cord or blade, the magnesium version is lighter, and that reduces fatigue over a long day. Against the Makita 5377MG at 13.2 lb it is similar in weight but with simpler maintenance. It is the standard tool for a framer.

Worm drive saws need gear oil changes. Follow the schedule in the manual and check the oil level every few months. Keep a spare blade on hand, since a dull blade is the most common cause of motor strain.
products.bestFor: Framers who want a classic worm drive in a lighter body.
pros: Lightest magnesium worm drive in the line
15 amp motor delivers strong torque
Cut-ready depth system speeds setup
Blade on the left gives a clear line

products.name: Makita 5377MG 7-1/4 Inch Magnesium Hypoid Saw
products.description:
The Makita 5377MG uses hypoid gears, which have more surface contact than a standard worm gear, and a sealed oil bath housing with a built-in fan that coats the gears. It weighs 13.2 lb and cuts 2-3/8 inches deep at 90 degrees. Positive bevel stops sit at 22.5, 45 and 51.5 degrees.

Compared with the SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 it has the same overall layout and slightly better lubrication design. Against the Bosch CSW41 it has more bevel stops and a more refined gear housing. It is a long lived tool for daily framing.

The sealed gear housing means less frequent maintenance. Check the oil periodically and keep the guard clean. The sealed housing also keeps sawdust out of the gears, which prolongs life on dusty sites.
products.bestFor: Framers who value gearing durability and low maintenance.
pros: Hypoid gears have more surface contact
Sealed oil bath reduces maintenance
Three bevel stops including 51.5 degrees
Magnesium parts keep weight at 13.2 lb
cons: Higher price than basic worm drives

products.name: Bosch CSW41 7-1/4 Inch Worm Drive Circular Saw
products.description:
The Bosch CSW41 has a 15 amp motor with a no-load speed of 5,300 rpm and a magnesium body that holds weight to 13.2 lb. The blade is on the left for a clear sight line, and the worm drive design provides accuracy and torque. It is a smooth, balanced tool.

Compared with the SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 it costs less and weighs about the same. Against the Makita 5377MG it lacks the oil bath housing, so maintenance is more regular. It is a solid choice for a carpenter who wants worm drive power without a premium.

Check the gear oil level, keep the guard clean and replace the brushes when worn. Compared with a name brand premium, the saving is real, but check the oil level more often.
products.bestFor: Carpenters who want a worm drive at a lower price.
pros: 15 amp motor with 5,300 rpm
Magnesium body keeps weight at 13.2 lb
Blade on the left helps visibility
Lower cost than premium worm drives

products.name: SKILSAW SPT78W-01 15 Amp 8-1/4 Inch Aluminum Worm Drive Saw
products.description:
The SPT78W-01 uses an 8-1/4 inch blade, which cuts deeper than the 7-1/4 inch saws, and a 15 amp Dual-Field motor built for saws. Its bevel capacity of 60 degrees is the largest here. An anti-snag lower guard handles small offcuts smoothly.

Compared with the SPT77WML-01 it has a bigger blade and more bevel, but weighs more. It suits cutting 4x lumber in one pass. It is a good fit for timber framers and builders who cut thick stock.

Bigger blades cost more and are less common. Keep the gear oil topped up and the guard moving freely. Make sure your blade guard clears the larger blade on small offcuts.
products.bestFor: Builders cutting thick timber in a single pass.
pros: 8-1/4 inch blade cuts deeper
60 degree bevel is the largest here
Anti-snag guard works on small offcuts
Dual-Field motor made for saws

products.name: DeWalt DCS577B FlexVolt 60V MAX 7-1/4 Inch Worm Drive Style Saw
products.description:
The DCS577B is a cordless saw with a worm drive style layout: blade on the left of the motor and the handle at the rear. It runs on FlexVolt batteries, and an electric brake stops the blade quickly. Bevel capacity is 53 degrees with stops at 22.5 and 45 degrees.

It does not use a worm gear, so it is quieter and needs no oil changes. Compared with the Milwaukee M18 FUEL rear handle saw it is a close rival, with the same cordless freedom. Against the corded SKILSAW it has less sustained power but no cord.

It is a bare tool, so budget for FlexVolt batteries. A large pack gives the longest run time. Because the layout copies a worm drive, the handling is familiar to framers who switch from corded saws.
products.bestFor: Framers who want worm drive ergonomics without a cord.
pros: Worm drive style layout with no cord
Electric brake stops the blade quickly
FlexVolt batteries share with other tools
No gear oil to maintain

products.name: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 7-1/4 Inch Rear Handle Circular Saw

specList.label: Run claim
specList.value: Up to 700 cuts with a 12.0 Ah pack

products.description:
The Milwaukee M18 FUEL rear handle saw has a segmented brushless motor that Milwaukee says delivers up to 20 percent more power, and it cuts 2-5/8 inches deep. The maker claims up to 700 cuts per charge with a 12.0 Ah battery. The rear handle layout copies the worm drive stance.

Compared with the DeWalt DCS577B it has deeper cut capacity, and the choice depends on your battery platform. Against corded worm drives it offers freedom from cords, though sustained rips in wet lumber drain the pack. It is a strong cordless option for framers.

Buy large batteries to match. Keep the guard clean and use a sharp framing blade. A rafter hook and an LED light are useful extras for roof work.
products.bestFor: Milwaukee M18 owners who want a rear handle framing saw.
pros: 2-5/8 inch cut capacity
Brushless motor with strong power
Rear handle suits framing posture
Up to 700 cuts claim with a large pack

buyingCriteria.explanation: A worm drive saw sits the motor behind the blade and uses a gear pair at right angles, which gives more torque and a longer, narrower body. A sidewinder is lighter and faster. The SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 and Makita 5377MG are worm and hypoid saws weighing about 13 lb. If you cut mostly softwood crosscuts, a sidewinder is easier. A common mistake is to assume more torque always means a better saw. A worm drive turns the blade a little slower than a sidewinder, which is why it feels calm in a rip but takes longer on a crosscut.

A hypoid gear, as on the Makita 5377MG, has more surface contact than a conventional worm gear and runs in a sealed oil bath. That reduces maintenance. Worm gears need oil changes. Choose hypoid if you want less upkeep. Oil bath housings coat the gears with a fan driven spray, and that is the reason the Makita runs cooler on long rips. If you hate maintenance chores, the sealed design is worth a modest premium.

Magnesium bodies cut weight to about 13.2 lb on the Bosch CSW41 and Makita, while aluminum versions like the SKILSAW SPT77W-01 weigh 14.2 lb without blade or cord. Lighter saws fatigue you less on a roof. A heavier saw is steadier in a rip. On a roof or a ladder, the 1 lb difference between a magnesium and an aluminum body is noticeable by the end of the day. Weigh the saw with the blade and a battery or cord attached for a fair comparison.

A 7-1/4 inch blade cuts about 2-3/8 inches deep on the Makita 5377MG. The SKILSAW SPT78W-01 uses an 8-1/4 inch blade for deeper cuts. The Milwaukee M18 FUEL rear handle cuts 2-5/8 inches. Match depth to the stock you cut. Set the blade depth about 1/4 inch beyond the board, and remember that a bigger blade cuts deeper but also puts more of the blade out of the guard. Wider blades also need more power.

A left side blade, as on the Bosch CSW41 and DeWalt DCS577B, gives right handed users a clear view of the cut line. Left handers may prefer a right side blade. Test the saw in your hands before you buy. Left handers often prefer a saw whose blade sits on the right, so they can see the cut. Check which side the blade is on before you order.

Corded worm drives offer constant power, while the DeWalt DCS577B and Milwaukee M18 FUEL give freedom from cords. A cordless saw needs large batteries for sustained cuts. Consider your jobsite power access. Cordless saws spend most of their charge on long rips, so match the battery size to your longest cut. A 12 Ah pack can run a day of framing, while a 5 Ah pack may need swapping at lunch.

specDecoder.meaning: A gear arrangement where a screw shaped gear meshes with a wheel gear, giving a torque boost and a narrow body. It needs oil.
specDecoder.watchFor: Gear oil changes are required on most designs.

specDecoder.meaning: A refined bevel gear with offset axes and more tooth contact. The Makita 5377MG uses it with an oil bath.
specDecoder.watchFor: Do not confuse hypoid with worm gearing, since service differs.

specDecoder.meaning: A SKILSAW motor with a second winding path that improves cooling. It extends motor life.
specDecoder.watchFor: It is a brand feature, not an industry standard.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: Constant power and no battery cost. The SKILSAW saws, Makita and Bosch fit here.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: Freedom from cords with worm drive layouts. The DeWalt DCS577B and Milwaukee M18 FUEL fit here.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for shop rips and cordless for roofs and remote jobs.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A saw with a rear handle, a clear line of sight and strong torque. Framing involves long cuts in wet lumber. Weight under 14 lb helps.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 and Makita 5377MG are best. The DeWalt DCS577B offers cordless freedom.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You frame daily or want low maintenance. The Makita 5377MG repays the cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cut a few boards a year. The Bosch CSW41 is enough.

maintenance.why: Worm gears need clean oil to avoid wear. Old oil causes heat and noise.
Low oil damages gears quickly. Top up as needed.
A sticky guard is a safety risk. Clean it often.
Worn brushes lose power. Replace them in pairs.
A dull blade strains the motor and gears.

faq.q: What is a worm drive circular saw?
faq.a: A saw that drives the blade through worm gears, giving more torque and a longer body. The blade sits on the left.

faq.q: Are worm drives better than sidewinders?
faq.a: For long rips and wet lumber, often yes. For crosscuts and light work, sidewinders are lighter.

faq.q: Do worm drive saws need oil?
faq.a: Yes. Most need gear oil changes, while hypoid saws with oil baths need less.

faq.q: Why is the blade on the left?
faq.a: It gives right handed users a clear view of the cut line. Left handers may prefer a right side blade.

faq.q: Are cordless rear handle saws as good?
faq.a: They come close. The DeWalt DCS577B and Milwaukee M18 FUEL work well but drain batteries in sustained cuts.
A 24 tooth framing blade for lumber. Use a finer blade for plywood.
